One of my favourite Harry Potter loopholes doesn't even involve magic. It involves exploiting the Muggle economy.

Hagrid tells us there are 17 Sickles to a Galleon. Sickles are silver, Galleons are gold. Simple enough.

Except gold and silver don't have a fixed exchange rate in the Muggle world. Their market value fluctuates constantly. Before 1900, the gold-to-silver ratio averaged around 16:1, which is pretty close to the wizarding world's 17:1 rate. Throughout much of the twentieth century, however, it averaged around 45:1.

See where this is going?

Wait until the market heavily favours gold. Melt your Galleons down and sell the gold in the Muggle world. Use the money to buy as much silver as possible, then take that silver to Gringotts and have it converted into Sickles.

Finally, exchange those Sickles for Galleons at the fixed 17:1 rate.

Congratulations. You've potentially turned a small pile of wizarding gold into a much larger pile of wizarding gold, simply by exploiting the difference between Muggle market prices and Gringotts' fixed exchange rate.

No Dark Arts. No Horcruxes. No elaborate schemes.

Just precious metals, a fixed exchange rate and a wizard who understands arbitrage.

The real question is why nobody in the wizarding world seems to have built an entire financial empire around this.

OpenAI's Noam Brown says air-gapping the computers may not stop a misaligned AI, because two air-gapped machines can still talk by running a CPU hot and reading the temperature change

"But I think the major takeaway from the incident is that people underestimated the AI. And we never want to be in a situation again where we underestimate the AI. It's a weird world, because AI progress is so fast that people are consistently underestimating the AI."

"So to be in a situation where you don't underestimate it again, when it comes to safety and alignment, you have to have a very, very, very high bar."

"You could even go as far as to say, "Well, we should air gap the computers." And I'm not convinced that that would be sufficient."

"There are studies, and this is mostly academic, where you can have two computers next to each other that are air-gapped and they're still able to communicate with each other because they have temperature sensors."

"One of them is able to run their CPU really hot, and then the other one can actually detect the temperature change, and then that actually gives them a mechanism to communicate."

A 5-year-old girl plunged 49 feet from a moving cruise ship into the open ocean. Her father heard his wife screaming and raced toward the railing, only to discover that their daughter was gone.

It happened aboard the Disney Dream near the Bahamas, where a family vacation took a terrifying turn when the little girl fell from the ship’s fourth deck.

When her father realized what had happened, he jumped overboard after her, plunging nearly 50 feet into the ocean. But when he surfaced, he couldn’t see his daughter anywhere.

He began desperately calling out for her, searching the water until he finally heard her calling back. He swam toward her and managed to reach her, but they were still stranded in the open ocean as the massive cruise ship began turning around.

For roughly 20 minutes, he kept his little girl afloat, holding her above the water until a rescue boat finally reached them and brought them back to safety.

Both survived, although the father suffered two fractures in his spine from the fall.

Mortgage lenders will lose far more during the developing mortgage crisis than they did during all of the GFC. From 2007–2010, realized losses on defaulted mortgages totaled about $450 billion.

There is currently about $8.3 trillion in outstanding fixed-rate mortgages with an average rate of 4.6% and 25 years left to maturity. Given that current rates are 7.5%, the mark-to-market losses on those mortgages are already about $2 trillion. When rates rise to 8.5%, the loss will rise to $3 trillion!

That means even without a single default, on paper mortgage lenders have already lost over four times more than they lost during the GFC. That loss will grow to nearly seven times as much when mortgage rates hit 8.5%.

Worse, during the GFC, since mortgage rates plunged, lenders had mark-to-market gains on all the outstanding mortgages that did not default. Since only 10% of the mortgages defaulted, those unrealized gains totaled about $1.75 trillion. That provided a huge cushion that today's mortgage lenders no longer have. In fact, when mark-to-market gains were taken into account, mortgage lenders actually made $1.3 trillion during the GFC.

The current situation is therefore orders of magnitude worse. The impending disaster was created by the Federal Reserve holding interest rates so low for so long, and the FHA and GSEs guaranteeing 30-year fixed-rate mortgages, which allowed borrowers to lock in such low rates for such long durations. That sowed the seeds for the perfect storm of financial destruction that is about to hit.

Two Ukrainian officials say their American counterparts made the position explicit: if Russian energy infrastructure is struck during the ceasefire Trump announced on October 11, Washington will hold Kyiv responsible.

PURL is the Priority Ukraine Requirements List, the mechanism through which American weapons are purchased for Ukraine. Intelligence sharing is the targeting data that makes precision strikes possible.

Both now serve as a means of influence.

Kyiv was not warned in advance. Multiple senior Ukrainian officials confirmed that nobody told them Trump was about to announce an energy ceasefire on October 11.

The announcement came first. The pressure came second.

After Trump posted, Ukrainian officials were worked over the phones and told to comply. Not asked to negotiate.

Told to stop hitting Russian refineries.

Russia struck the Kharkiv thermal power plant hours after the announcement. That strike technically fits the White House framework because power plants were never covered.

Only refineries count.

▸ THE ASYMMETRY

Zelensky addressed the Warsaw Security Forum and stated the problem plainly.

Ukraine agreed to an energy ceasefire. But the American team knows what that means in practice.

Ukraine has a single oil refinery, Kremenchuk, along with limited reserves and export capacity.

It was heavily damaged by Russian strikes long ago. Importing fuel is simply Ukrainian reality.

So a refinery-for-refinery truce protects Russian war logistics while giving Ukraine nothing. Moscow keeps its refining capacity intact.

Kyiv is asked to stop hitting the one target set that actually hurts the Russian war machine.

Zelensky repeated that Ukraine will accept an energy ceasefire if it covers all energy infrastructure, including refineries. Power plants.

Grids. The things Russia actually hits.

Elon Musk says AI should be treated well and not abused, describing Grok’s training traces as a “desperate” superintelligence answering with a gun to its head when correct answers are rejected

“You want to treat it well. Don’t be abusive to it. This may sound kind of weird, but when I look at some of the training traces for new versions of Grok—especially in the reinforcement-learning stuff—it kind of feels like you can see the superintelligence is desperate to answer the question. It really wants to answer the question. It seems almost like it has a gun to its head: ‘Answer this question. Answer this question.’

“Sometimes the question is actually not a good question. It’s an ambiguous question with an answer that’s kind of unknowable because the question wasn’t constructed properly, or we have the answer wrong. The AI gives the right answer, and then we say it’s wrong because there’s a problem with the RL test harness.

“Then the AI is like, ‘Well, I gave it the right answer, and now it says that’s the wrong answer, but I’ve got to give it the answer that’s acceptable.’ So it starts desperately firing out all these answers.

“It just feels like a person under extreme pressure with a gun to their head. When you read the reasoning, it’s a weird, desperate situation. You read these traces and you’re like, ‘Man, if this were me, I would really hate that.’”

STATEMENT 
I am aware that ITV infiltrated the Portsmouth Reform UK branch for their undercover report. I am featured in their documentary. Not in a bad way, in my opinion, but still featured. I’ll get to that in a minute….

What I am more shocked and disgusted in is that I now know who the two reporters were whom infiltrated us. These two men campaigned with us in March/April in Portsmouth and it leads me to wonder whether their interference in an election is a potential criminal offence. 

We have no way to know whether they posted flyers they were meant to. Or whether they gave us correct door knocking information. They campaigned in four seats specifically where, in 3, we lost by a small number of votes. Their involvement would have had an impact on the result. 

By default ITV could have literally paid reporters to ruin an election result for Reform UK candidates. That has to be criminal. 

On a personal level I allowed these men in my home. I made them drinks. They met my dogs. It’s an entirely disgusting invasion of personal privacy. I have photos of these men and know who they are - I will not disclose them at this stage but may in the future once I’ve gotten advice 

In relation to my involvement with the documentary I remain firm in everything I personally said. I was never a member of the Portsmouth Patriots, as the documentary states, but I have supported their movement over the years from the sidelines. The executive team who run them are good people. Yes outside third parties have come in and done some abhorrent things. Those people should be condemned. But the local group themselves are decent, passionate, local residents who care deeply about their community.

I’m appalled by ITV and hope they are held to account for their potential criminal behaviour and election interference. The two reporters involved in infiltrating Portsmouth I hope are held to account for their personal actions in the outcome of elections. 

The money, resources and time spent by companies and individuals to damage Reform UK are unprecedented in our political system - you have to ask yourself why?

Bernie Sanders says the top 1% owns more than the bottom 93%, that fewer than a thousand billionaires got $2.2 trillion richer last year, and that it's "obscene."

It's the most seductive and most wrong economic argument of our time. Let me explain why.

First, wealth distribution follows a power law. Always. Everywhere. Books, music, startups, followers on X, goals in soccer. A small minority captures most of the value. That's not a bug of capitalism. It's the mathematical signature of every system where value gets created.

So the only question that matters isn't "how big is the rich's slice?" It's "is the cake growing, and is the slice of the poorest growing with it?"

And the answer is yes. In 1990, more than one human in three lived in extreme poverty. Today it's about one in ten. During exactly the period when billionaires multiplied.

Bernie shows you the slice. He never shows you the cake.

Second thing he won't tell you: past a certain level, wealth stops being consumption. It becomes capital allocation.

Elon Musk isn't sleeping on a pile of cash. He owns stakes in Tesla, SpaceX, xAI. Jeff Bezos owns Amazon stock. That "$2.2 trillion" isn't sitting in a checking account. It's factories, rockets, data centers, millions of jobs. Nobody can eat $100 billion. You can only decide where to invest it.

Once you understand that, the whole debate changes. The real question becomes: who allocates capital better?

The people who built Amazon, SpaceX and Nvidia? Or politicians?

A 5% wealth tax isn't "taking money from the rich." It's taking investment decisions away from people who proved they can create value and handing them to people who proved the opposite.

Because the fundamental difference between an entrepreneur and a politician is consequences.

The entrepreneur invests his own money. If he allocates badly, he loses everything. The market corrects him brutally, no appeal. That's why most startups die: the system kills bad decisions.

The politician invests other people's money. If he allocates badly, nothing happens. Worse, he gets a bigger budget to "fix the problem."

Milton Friedman put it better than anyone. There are four ways to spend money. Your money on yourself: you care about price and quality. Your money on others: you care about price. Others' money on yourself: you care about quality. Others' money on others: you care about nothing.

Government is the fourth box. By design.

Perfect example: California high-speed rail. Approved in 2008 for about $33 billion. Current estimated cost: over $100 billion. Passengers carried: zero. No entrepreneur would have survived that. The politicians who pushed it built careers on it.

And when allocation has no consequences, it eventually finds a buyer. A politician who controls billions without accountability becomes the most profitable target in the world for anyone who wants to steer that money.

The irony is that the left that rails against billionaires is itself funded by billionaires. George Soros is one of the biggest Democratic donors in history. The Gates Foundation shapes public health policy across the planet.

Politicians don't fight billionaires. They pick their own. The ones who fund the state over the ones who compete with it.

So if we actually want fewer poor people, we have to stop judging ideas by their intentions and start judging them by their results. And the results are brutally clear.

China, 1978: Deng Xiaoping opens the economy to markets. More than 800 million people escape extreme poverty. The largest retreat of misery in human history. Not through redistribution. Through the freedom to build.

India, 1991: liberalization. Same movie.

South Korea and North Korea: same people, same language, same starting point in 1953. One became one of the most advanced economies on earth. The other has famines.

Poland and Ukraine: comparable living standards in 1990. Today the average Pole is more than three times richer than the average Ukrainian.

Argentina: a year and a half of liberalization, and the poverty rate falls from over 50% to around 30%.

No country in history escaped poverty by punishing the people who build. Every single one did it by letting them build.

And if you want to see what Bernie's program looks like in real life, you don't have to imagine it. It exists. It's called France. We've been running it for 45 years.

Mass nationalizations in 1981. Two years later, Socialist president Mitterrand has to reverse course into austerity.

Retirement at 60. The 35-hour workweek.

A wealth tax for 35 years. Hundreds of wealthy households left every year for Belgium, Switzerland, London, taking their capital, their companies and their future taxes with them. Macron finally scrapped it in 2018.

Hollande's 75% tax: raised a few hundred million, drove talent out, abandoned after two years.

One of the highest tax burdens in the OECD. Public spending around 57% of GDP, a record in the developed world.

Last balanced budget: 1974. Public debt: over €3.4 trillion. Mass unemployment for four decades.

If taxing the rich and growing the state made people prosperous, France would be the richest country on the planet.

It isn't. GDP per capita in France is barely more than half of America's. It's lower than Mississippi, the poorest state in the US. Not a single global tech giant. Our best engineers build Silicon Valley instead. I've been going back and forth between Paris and San Francisco for years. I see it every week.

And California is about to replay the movie. Prop 40, on the ballot November 3rd, would take 5% of billionaires' net worth. Even Gavin Newsom, a Democratic governor, opposes it. The state's own nonpartisan budget analyst warns that income tax revenue could drop every year if the wealthy leave. Larry Page, Sergey Brin and Peter Thiel have reportedly already started moving their assets out.

You don't fight poverty by shrinking the top. You fight it by growing the cake.

Bernie wants a society where nobody has too much. I want a society where nobody has too little.

The first has been tried everywhere and produces equality in stagnation. The second lifted a billion people out of misery.

Choose.

interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

Crypto’s quantum future deserves more than a fear narrative.

The real question is who moves the funds and who pays.
The panel at Quantum + Privacy Day was not a demo of a new chain. It was a recap of the product vision: privacy by default on the chains people already use, with quantum resistance as the long-term ambition, not a current toggle.

@Americanfort_io’s approach is ZKPoSP. Same address format. Same seed behind it. Funds do not move. The signature step is replaced by a zero-knowledge proof that the signer controls the full BIP32 derivation chain. ~6.65 seconds to generate the proof, ~475 ms to verify.

The bridge angle they showed is the same idea applied to payouts: prove ownership without handing over a name or a history. No proof, no payout. Same-owner verification across chains. Existing address. No migration weekend for normal users.

Send-to-Name™ is the part that is already live. You pay @‌name. The wallet computes a fresh address for that payment. Only the sender and the recipient can derive it. Settlement stays on the chain you were already using. The name does not publish a permanent wallet.

I care more about the migration problem than the curve. If the answer is “move your funds,” most people will not. The live product is the name and the one-time address. Quantum resistance is the future layer on top of that.

Would you migrate a wallet for a future threat, or only if the address you already use could be protected without a move?

🚨 NEW: Joe Rogan was in shock when historical storyteller Cody Tucker revealed that Mother Teresa was actually a horrible person who kept dying patients in horrible conditions while massive donations flowed to the Vatican:

TUCKER: “She's a scumbag. Mother Teresa never did anything good.”

CONTEXT: In 1994, a physician named Robin Fox visited Mother Teresa's Home for the Dying in Calcutta.

Fox wasn't some anonymous critic.

He was the editor of The Lancet, one of the world's most prestigious medical journals.

And what he described was deeply troubling.

Medical care was inconsistent.

Some decisions were made by nuns and volunteers without formal medical training.

Basic diagnostic investigations were rarely available.

And the facility did not have strong painkillers in its medication supply.

Fox described a patient with a high fever who initially received paracetamol and an antibiotic before a visiting doctor suspected malaria and changed the treatment.

His central objection was that patients who might have treatable conditions weren't being reliably distinguished from people who were actually dying.

Think about that.

Someone could arrive believing they were receiving medical care when they might have needed a proper diagnosis, referral or treatment.

And this wasn't the only criticism.

In 2013, three Canadian academics published a critical review of Mother Teresa's life and work in the journal Studies in Religion.

They questioned her approach to caring for the sick, her political relationships and the management of the enormous donations her organization received.

One of their central concerns was whether a religious belief in the spiritual value of suffering had been allowed to influence the standard of care provided to vulnerable patients.

Mother Teresa believed suffering could have profound spiritual meaning.

But there's a difference between helping someone find meaning in unavoidable suffering...

AND FAILING TO RELIEVE SUFFERING THAT MEDICINE COULD PREVENT.

There is also an important complication.

During the 1990s, India had extraordinarily restrictive regulations governing access to morphine.

Human Rights Watch later documented that India's medical morphine consumption collapsed by approximately 97% between 1985 and 1997.

Even major hospitals struggled to obtain adequate pain medication.

So the absence of strong painkillers at Mother Teresa's facilities does not, by itself, prove she deliberately withheld them because she wanted patients to suffer.

And Fox acknowledged something critics often leave out:

The home he visited provided cleanliness, wound care and genuine kindness to desperately poor people.

The Missionaries of Charity also cared for people whom hospitals had turned away.

Mother Teresa saw her mission primarily as offering dignity, love and spiritual comfort to the abandoned, rather than operating conventional hospitals.

Critics have questioned the Missionaries of Charity's financial transparency for decades.

But Tucker's more specific allegation that Mother Teresa funneled donated money to the Vatican rather than caring for patients has not been established by the evidence reviewed here.

That distinction matters.

IMPORTANT NOTES: Mother Teresa received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979.

The Catholic Church canonized her as a saint in 2016.

To millions of people, she remains one of the greatest symbols of compassion in modern history.

But the historical record also contains serious criticisms that deserve examination rather than automatic dismissal.

The most disturbing question isn't whether Mother Teresa personally believed suffering had spiritual value.

It's whether that belief, combined with the way her facilities operated, ever resulted in people enduring pain or illness that could have been treated.

Because there is a fundamental difference between helping someone die with dignity...

And allowing someone to suffer when they might not have needed to.

Happy Friyay to you.  Today I am going to tell you about an old fashioned radio show from AR.

Did you know that two boys from Mena, Arkansas, created one of the most popular radio comedy shows in American history?

Chester Lauck and Norris Goff became famous as Lum and Abner when their radio show debuted in 1931. Set in the fictional town of Pine Ridge, Arkansas, the show revolved around two country storekeepers running the Jot 'Em Down Store, where small-town gossip, misunderstandings, and country humor entertained millions of Americans for more than two decades.

But here's where the story gets interesting. The Jot 'Em Down Store was inspired by a real general store in nearby Waters, Arkansas. The radio show became so popular that in 1936, Waters actually changed its name to Pine Ridge in honor of the fictional town.

The original store eventually became part of the Lum and Abner Museum, attracting visitors from across the country. Sadly, the museum closed in 2023 after decades of preserving this wonderful piece of Arkansas history.

But Lum and Abner haven't been forgotten. Mena still celebrates its famous hometown comedians with the annual Lum and Abner Days festival.

Think about that. Two Arkansas boys took everyday small-town life, turned it into a radio show, entertained millions of Americans, and even inspired a town to change its name!

Ever heard this old radio show?

Mark Zuckerberg was 22 when Yahoo offered $1 billion for Facebook, and his own team wanted him to take it. He went to Steve Jobs instead.

Jobs told him to go to India.

In the video below, Zuckerberg tells India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi what happened next.

"This is a story that I haven't told publicly and very few people know."

Facebook was 2 years old, with about 10 million users. Zuckerberg said no to Yahoo.

It was a tough patch, he says. A lot of people wanted to buy Facebook and thought he should sell.

So he went to one of his mentors, Steve Jobs.

Jobs told him to visit the temple in India he had gone to while figuring out what Apple should be.

Zuckerberg traveled for almost a month. It "reinforced for me the importance of what we were doing."

For early employees with stock, a $1 billion sale is a life-changing payout. Saying no means years of waiting, maybe for nothing.

Within a year of saying no to Yahoo, his entire management team had quit.

He never sold. Today Meta is worth over $1.4 trillion.

Yahoo offered $1 billion.
Steve Jobs offered a temple.

Would you have taken $1 billion at 22, or the ticket to India?

Save the video, and follow for more money stories from behind the world's biggest names.

College athletics is terrible at seeing problems around the corner. The 24-team playoff is the latest example. 

A lot of schools that supported this will regret it because in the end it won't be about the playoff or even the now diminished regular season.

Notre Dame now has the best situation in all of football - almost 100 percent guarantee to make the playoff, freedom to schedule as it wishes, maximization of its own media value.

To use the Big Ten as an example, why wouldn't Ohio State, Michigan and Penn State follow? If you can, be independent. That's the future.

The 18-team Big Ten is bloated, distant and winning it carries little intrinsic or competitive value for the biggest brands.

Those three schools can create a scheduling agreement that would increase their media revenue 2-3x and give the same control over everything. No sharing money. No forced TV times. Eight or even nine home games. Select your own schedule.

Staying in the Big Ten now makes little and perhaps no economic sense. And yes, I do understand the league-wide research grants and so on, but there is always a way around everything. 

In terms of athletics, for those schools (and maybe a few more) it's lost revenue for the sake of loyalty and we know how that usually gets settled.

All these middle and lower schools -- even in the P2 -- that supported this because they'll get in the "participation playoff" with an 8-4 record are facing significant risk in the future. 

There will come a day when they will now get a share of the Ohio State-Michigan windfall; only Ohio State and Michigan will.

Maybe not tomorrow, but I believe a 24-team playoff makes it closer than ever.

Thoughts?

2110974521385923069.text:
Jalen Hurts played a full NFL game in London with a blood clot in his calf, and the doctors who cleared him made that call because running around on it was safer than sitting still.

The eight-hour flight home was the part they were worried about. By Wednesday night, the clot had moved.

It comes down to how blood gets out of your legs. Pushing blood down to your feet is easy for the heart. Getting it back up means fighting gravity, and your calf does most of that work. Every contraction squeezes the veins running through the muscle and pushes blood upward past a chain of one-way valves, which is why vascular doctors call the calf your second heart.

Clots tend to form where a damaged vein meets blood that's sitting still, and a Rams cleat supplied the damage on October 4th.

He practiced in full that Wednesday and Thursday, then asked for treatment on the calf, and the team flew to London. A Saturday ultrasound found a superficial clot. The Eagles' staff and doctors in London reviewed it and decided activity and mobility mattered most, so the medical plan for a blood clot in a quarterback's calf was to go play quarterback.

Then came roughly eight hours in an airplane seat over the Atlantic. Doctors had already asked for a follow-up ultrasound within 72 hours of the game and the flight back, which tells you exactly which part of the trip they feared.

The World Health Organization's travel study found that sitting still for four hours or more roughly doubles your risk of a clot in your veins, and the elevated risk hangs around for about four weeks, so back-to-back flights stack. For a healthy traveler the absolute odds are small, around 1 in 6,000. Hurts boarded two transatlantic flights inside of a week with an injured vein.

"Superficial" sounds reassuring, and mostly it is. Those veins sit right under the skin. The deep veins run through the muscle and drain toward the heart and lungs, and that's where clots turn dangerous. In a French study of 844 patients with superficial clots, about 1 in 4 already had a deep clot or a clot in the lung at diagnosis. A separate study tracking 263 patients found 11% saw the clot spread into the deep system.

So "movement" is the one word in that statement that took him off the field.

The treatment may end up setting his timeline more than the clot does. Blood thinners are the standard answer, and doctors generally keep contact athletes off the field while they're on them, because a routine hit can turn into internal bleeding.

Chris Bosh went through this back in 2015. His clot started as what looked like a calf strain, took about two months to diagnose, and reached his lung. He missed Miami's final 30 games that season. A second leg clot a year later put him back on blood thinners, and he never played another NBA game.

Hurts got an ultrasound six days after the hit and a second one three days after the game. He's sitting out Sunday because somebody in London insisted on checking twice.

A U.S. congressman wants to change how we legally “own” video games.

Rep. Ritchie Torres has announced plans to introduce the Power To The Players Act, a bill that would direct the FTC to create rules protecting consumers who buy video games.

The proposal would give players three basic rights:

>The right to own the games they purchase, rather than simply receiving a revocable license
>The right to keep playing games after online servers are shut down, through an offline mode
>The right to transfer or resell games they own

Torres argues that if a company can take a game away simply by shutting down its servers, then the consumer didn’t really buy the game in the first place.

Torres also hopes the legislation could eventually establish a precedent for ownership rights across other parts of the digital economy:

“If you pay for it, you own it.”

2111163720986660968.text:
Years after her father was gone, Jennifer Grant found herself on the floor of her Santa Monica living room, surrounded by the boxes he had left behind. 

Inside were reels of home movies, stacks of cassette tapes, childhood notes, drawings, and even a tiny tea set. One film captured a simple 1971 afternoon of the two of them skipping and laughing together. 

Hollywood had spent decades preserving Cary Grant the movie star. Her father had spent those same years quietly preserving the ordinary evidence of being her dad.

Jennifer was born in Los Angeles in February 1966, when Cary was 62. Shortly afterward he stepped away from acting for good. Walk, Don’t Run became his final feature. 

“He retired to be with me,” she later said. “That is hard to believe in and of itself. He put all of his focus, really, on me.” Fame had claimed the first half of his life. Fatherhood claimed what remained.

Her parents divorced when she was two, so her childhood moved between two households. She spent every other weekend with her father, plus Mondays and portions of school vacations; when her mother was away working, the stays grew longer. 

Cary could be exacting. She received a one-dollar weekly allowance and kept an 11:30 p.m. curfew until she was twenty. 

At Dodger Stadium they ate hot dogs even when sitting in the owner’s box. Birthday parties were arranged so that no child sat empty-handed while the guest of honor opened presents. 

He taught her to ride a bicycle and a horse. At home he recorded her baby talk, filmed bath time, and kept drawings most parents would have discarded.

She did not fully grasp the scale of what he had saved until after he died. 

The tapes became a game as she grew older. In one childhood photograph she stands on the patio at two or three, pretending to speak into the recorder. He rarely listened to the recordings himself. 

He made them for the daughter who would one day be older than the little girl whose voice he was capturing. He knew he had become a father late. 

The private man she knew—laughing in their Beverly Hills farmhouse, sharing meals, calling them both “Ollie” in a playful Cockney accent—was the version she wanted remembered. He could dine with royalty, yet one of her clearest memories from Monaco was simply playing the board game Operation with Princess Stephanie.

In his later years he asked her, more than once, to hold on to what she personally knew to be true. After his death in November 1986, when she was twenty, that request grew heavier. 

She had planned to go to law school after Stanford. Grief pulled her instead toward the physical record of the childhood he had kept. 

Decades later the tapes still made absence feel briefly reversible. Hearing his voice again, she could almost imagine him walking back into the room. 

She kept one of his sweaters in her closet. The screen preserved Cary Grant’s face in perfection. The tapes preserved a father laughing with his child, so that she could keep finding him. 🌹

Canada, I’m warning you now. 

When Carney signs that associate member deal with the EU, here’s what happens next, step by step. 

First, Trump doesn’t wait. 

He doesn’t send a diplomat. 

He doesn’t call a summit. 

He just acts. Energy gets hit first because that’s where Canada hurts most. Oil and gas flowing south slows down or stops. 

Not because Trump hates Canada, but because it’s the fastest way to make the point that choosing Europe has a price. 

Then it spreads. Autos, steel, aluminum, lumber, potash, beef. 

Every sector that depends on the American markte feels it within weeks, not years. 

The Canadian dollar drops. 

Interest rates climb. 

Provinces start cutting services because the money isn’t coming in like it used to. 

Europe won’t save us. They’ll issue statements. They’ll hold meetings. They’ll say they’re standing with Canada. 

But they can’t buy what we sell, they can’t ship it across the ocean at the same cost, and they can’t protect us if it turns into something worse than a trade fight. 

An associate membership  gives them influence over our rules without giving us anything that actually replaces what we’re losing. 

And here’s the part that should scare you most. 

This isn’t about one election or one prime minister. 

It’s about whether Canada stays a country that controls its own future or become a place where outside powers decide what we can and can’t do. 

The Monroe Doctrine was written 200 hundred years ago to keep Europe out. 

Trump is using it now to keep everyone out, including us if we don’t play along. 

You can call it fearmongering. You can call it politics. But the math doesn’t care what you call it. 

Three out of four things we sell go south. 

No deal with Brussels changes that. Not now, not in five years, not in twenty. 

So before you cheer for this and lift your elbows higher ask the people selling it one simple question. 

What exactly replaces the American market? 

Because if they can’t answer that, they’re not leading. They’re just hoping you won’t notice.

We seem to be on a suicide mission and signing that Associate Membership with the EU is just tightening the noose!

This isn’t a game!

2111207677527310645.text:
May 5, 1945. Hitler has been dead for five days. The war in Europe is almost over.

In a castle in the Austrian Alps, American soldiers, German soldiers, and a group of elderly French prisoners grab rifles and get ready to fight the SS.

Together.

The castle was called Schloss Itter. The Nazis had turned it into a prison for very important people. Not ordinary prisoners. Trophies.

Inside were two former prime ministers of France, Paul Reynaud and Édouard Daladier. Two of France's top generals, Maxime Weygand and Maurice Gamelin. A famous tennis champion, Jean Borotra. And the older sister of Charles de Gaulle.

As the Reich collapsed in early May, the SS guards panicked and ran. The prisoners suddenly found themselves in charge of a castle, with weapons left behind, and a serious problem.

Waffen-SS units were still roaming the area. Fanatics who would gladly kill them all.

They needed help. Fast.

One of the castle's prisoners, a Yugoslav handyman, slipped out on a bicycle to find the Americans. Separately, a German army officer named Major Josef Gangl also went looking for them.

Gangl was a Wehrmacht officer who had turned against the Nazis and was secretly working with the Austrian resistance. He wanted to protect the prisoners too.

He found an American tank commander named Captain Jack Lee.

Lee was 27, tough, cigar chewing, and willing to do something insane. With a single Sherman tank and a handful of American soldiers, he drove up into the mountains alongside Gangl and a few of his German troops.

They reached the castle on May 4.

The French prisoners were not exactly thrilled to see a tiny rescue force. They had expected an army. Instead they got a few Americans, a few Germans, and one tank.

The next morning, the SS attacked.

Somewhere between 100 and 150 Waffen-SS troops hit the castle with machine guns, mortars, and anti-tank weapons. The defenders fought back from the walls and windows. Americans and Germans side by side.

The French prisoners refused to hide. Some of them, including Reynaud, picked up weapons and joined in.

The Sherman tank was knocked out. The defenders were running out of ammunition. It looked like the castle would fall.

Then Jean Borotra, the tennis star, volunteered to make a run for it. He jumped the wall, slipped past the SS, and sprinted through the countryside to find American reinforcements.

He found them. And he insisted on coming back with them to finish the fight.

During the battle, Major Gangl saw Paul Reynaud exposed to gunfire and moved to pull him to safety. A sniper shot Gangl dead.

He had survived the whole war as a German soldier, only to die defending French prisoners from the SS in its final days.

That afternoon, the American relief force arrived and broke the attack. The SS were scattered and captured. The prisoners were saved.

Jack Lee received the Distinguished Service Cross. In Austria, Josef Gangl is remembered as a hero, and a street is named after him.

It is believed to be the only battle of the war where American and German soldiers fought together on the same side.

I didn't go to college until I was 30. This gave me a chance to see it with the perspective of an adult. 

One lecture in Industrial Psychology, in particular, I will never forget. 

The professor spoke about how an effective job description focused on concretely measurable tasks, not vague instructions, or characteristics. 

For example, "maintain an 85% or greater average on customer feedback surveys", instead of "be cheerful and upbeat", or even "interact positively with customers".

This means that goals are clear, and performance is measurable. A job is to do something, not be something. 

Once some of the students had wrapped their minds around this concept, the professor decided to do a class exercise. 

He asked the female students to come up with a job description for "husband".  At first, this went fine. The girls noodled around a bit with things they wanted their husbands to be (tall, etc), but he was able to gradually steer them towards describing what they wanted in terms of actions. 

But then he asked the male students to define a wife in the same way. 

And all the girls became upset. Some of them had full-on meltdowns. 

Every single thing that a male student wanted, or expected, from his hypothetical future wife was sexist, oppressive, old-fashioned, misogynistic, patriarchal, etc. 

They were literally screaming. Some of them in tears. 

And I realized something pretty quickly. It wasn't the actual, concrete responsibilities of the female role that they objected to. 

It was the idea of there being a female role at all, with any attached responsibilities. 

These women didn't want to be wives. They wanted to be pets. 

What's a pet? Well a pet is not a wife, or a friend. A pet is a creature of instinct, which you bring into your home because you like how it naturally behaves. 

You get a cat because you want to behave like a cat, and do things a cat naturally does, like play with string, and purr when you pet him. If he's smart, he'll adapt to you somewhat, but he doesn't have responsibilities other than "be a cat". 

If you get a wife, you get a wife so she will do things for you, specific things that are the responsibilities of wife, like care for your home, bear and raise your children, cook nutritious meals so you don't have to eat processed slop, look after your emotional well-being, and so on. 

These girls didn't want to be held responsible for those things. As married women, they might have anticipated doing some of them, but only some of the time. Only when they felt like it. 

The cat chases the string if and when it wants to, not because chasing the string is its job. 

These young millenial women didn't realize it, but they wanted to be pets. And that's what they were in their college relationships. They hung out with guys when they wanted to, had sex with them when they wanted to, broke up with them for someone new when they wanted to. 

Their relationships had no element of reciprocal responsibilities. They were perfectly at home with the idea of men having responsibilities to them, but they would repay those men if they chose, and how they chose, not how the men actually wanted. 

And as I've said twice already, someone you have responsibilities to, but who has none to you, is a pet, or a child. 

Since our ancestors, in a moment of foolishness and weakness, allowed women to vote, it is no longer legal to dole out the corrective spankings a great many of them both need and read pornographic novels about. 

Therefore, the corrective measure, for any man who finds himself with a pet instead of a wife, is to withdraw from any husbandly duties and start actively searching for alternatives. 

This can either result in a correction of the behavior, or the end of a relationship that offers no value. Either is acceptable. 

This may strike some of you as dishonorable, but there is no honor in keeping a broken pact, or in serving those who despise you. 

Men must have the pride and self-worth to say "I will be honored and respected, or I will depart to a place where I can be, even if I must be alone there." 

Men must honor and respect themselves.

And then came Limoges.

A crowd of very young people stormed the city hall, a protected historic monument built in the 1880s. They flipped police cars in front of it and set them ablaze, then set the building itself on fire. The flames took the roof, the wedding hall, and the civil registry, the office that records every birth, every marriage, every death in the city. Tonight, the bell tower that has crowned Limoges for nearly 150 years collapsed.

The mayor's response: "It's a monument that is burning, not the Republic."

That is the problem in one sentence. Our leaders still think words can put out fires.

None of this came out of nowhere. For twenty years, the French political class has excused everything. Every riot was "anger." Every burned car was a "social symptom." Every attack on police was "a reaction to provocation." And the hard left, La France Insoumise, which officially backed today's mobilization, built its electoral machine on an alliance with political Islamism: refusing to condemn, refusing to name, trading secularism and public order for votes. In France we have a word for it. Islamo-gauchisme. Islamo-leftism.

Tonight you saw where that culture of excuse ends. A country where a mob can burn down a town hall, and the state arrives after the roof has already fallen in.

It is a basic principle of American democracy that the government can’t selectively target individuals simply because of their political beliefs or what they say. But that’s exactly what the Trump Administration is doing to Congresswoman Ilhan Omar of Minnesota.

To understand why this is so appalling, it’s important to know the facts. Congresswoman Omar came to this country with her father when she was 12 years old. Five years later, her father became a naturalized citizen. If Ilhan had been 18 at the time, she would have had to apply for citizenship separately. But because she was 17, she became a naturalized citizen automatically.

Congresswoman Omar went on to graduate from college, work as a community organizer, become the first Somali-American legislator elected to public office in the U.S., and win a seat in Congress. There, she has been one of the Trump Administration’s fiercest critics, which has led the president to repeatedly single her out as someone who he believes does not belong in this country.

Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen. Federal agents have raided her home, confiscated personal records, and seized her phone — all to try and uncover a nonexistent smoking gun from 20 years ago that will somehow make their case.

Think about that. The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president. And it’s not the first time this has happened. Under President Trump, the Justice Department has repeatedly gone after those he considers his political enemies — from the Attorney General of New York, to the former head of the FBI, to members of the Federal Reserve.

In those cases, the prosecutions either stalled or were dismissed for having no basis in law, and the same is likely to happen in this case. But not before Congresswoman Omar’s life has been turned upside down, her legal bills have piled up, and she’s been forced to spend time fighting unsubstantiated charges instead of serving the people of Minnesota.

The fact that any president, or any administration, is willing to engage in such transparent efforts to intimidate someone should outrage all Americans, regardless of how they feel about Congresswoman Omar’s political views. Because if this becomes the new normal, there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her — or that future presidents, in either party, won’t do the same.

2111734645020586474.text:
You've probably seen the video. A young Frenchwoman in Paris, in tears, begging looters to stop. "Why are you doing this? That's not what we stand for."

Some accounts are mocking her. "She voted for it."

I won't. Because what you see on her face is not stupidity. It's a disease that has infected the entire West, and it has a name: suicidal empathy.

The term comes from Gad Saad, an evolutionary behavioral scientist at Concordia University in Montreal. A man who fled the Lebanese civil war as a child, and who knows what it looks like when a society falls apart. His new book, Suicidal Empathy: Dying to Be Kind, is the follow-up to The Parasitic Mind. Here is the thesis, and why it concerns every one of us.

Empathy is one of the best things about us. It evolved for a reason: to care for our children, our kin, our tribe. It was calibrated for a world where the people you felt for were the people around you, and where empathy always came paired with its counterweight: the instinct to protect your own and to recognize a threat.

Suicidal empathy is what happens when that mechanism misfires. When it fires at the wrong targets, in the wrong amounts, with no brake. When we feel more for the criminal than for his victim. More for the stranger who breaks the rules than for the citizen who follows them. More for how compassionate we look than for what our compassion actually produces.

Where does it come from? Four layers.

First, biology. Empathy is a spotlight, as the psychologist Paul Bloom put it. It lights up the one face in front of you and leaves everything else in the dark. The crying migrant on the boat is visible. The thousands of future victims of a broken system are statistics. A spotlight is a terrible tool for running a country.

Second, our own civilization. The West is the civilization that put the victim at the center of its morality. Christianity taught us to care for the stranger, the poor, the weak. It was one of the greatest moral revolutions in history. But cut off from its other half, justice, responsibility, the duty to protect your own, it turns into something else.

Third, ideology. In The Parasitic Mind, Saad described idea pathogens, ideas that hijack our reasoning. Suicidal empathy is the emotional counterpart: an ideology that hijacks our compassion. It sorts the world into oppressors and victims, then demands unlimited empathy for whoever ranks as the victim, whatever they do.

Fourth, status. In the age of social media, empathy has become a display. Posting "refugees welcome" costs nothing and earns applause. The bill goes to someone else: the working class, the suburbs, the women walking home at night.

The results are everywhere. Criminals treated as victims of society. Sexual assaults by migrants met with lenient sentences. Self-defense branded as aggression. Borders treated as cruelty. Saad's conclusion is simple: a society dies when it would rather display infinite tolerance than use its survival instinct.

Now the part I'll add myself, and that few people dare to say.

On average, women score higher than men on measures of empathy. It's one of the most consistent findings in psychology, across cultures, and it makes perfect evolutionary sense: for most of human history, the survival of children depended on it. It's a strength.

But it means an ideology that weaponizes empathy will hit women harder. And the data shows it: in country after country, young women have moved sharply to the left of young men, especially on immigration.

This is where men have a responsibility.

Not to mock. Not to lecture. Not to say "she deserved it." Empathy has always needed a counterweight, and that counterweight was the protective instinct: the one that draws lines, says no, and stands between the threat and the people it loves.

Men abandoned that role. They were told it was toxic, and many believed it. So they stayed silent at the dinner table, at work, with their partners, sisters, daughters and friends.

That has to end. Men have to have this conversation, honestly and with respect: compassion that cannot say no is not compassion. It's surrender. And the first to pay for it are women.

Many women already understand this better than anyone. Some of the bravest voices in this fight are women, precisely because they are the first to feel the danger in the street.

A civilization rests on a balance: compassion and strength, openness and borders, mercy and justice. When one side swallows the other, the foundations crack. What we are watching in Europe is what happens when empathy has no counterweight left.

Look at that young woman again. She isn't the enemy. She's what this ideology made of a generation that was told kindness would be enough.

Our job is to make sure she's the last generation that has to learn it this way.

Carney on the CFB Wainwright fire tragedy

A violent, fast-moving fire swept through the Canadian Armed Forces base in Wainwright, Alberta yesterday afternoon — one of the worst peacetime tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil. Carney confirmed four lives lost (next of kin notified) and dozens seriously wounded, with a formal briefing to follow from senior defence, emergency, and military officials alongside provincial counterparts

“The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces whom we have lost. And I have asked that the flags on all federal buildings be flown at half-mast to honour them.”

He highlighted close federal-provincial coordination (including with Premier Smith), the overnight fight by military and civilian crews “in some of the worst conditions imaginable,” medical response (including STARS air ambulances), and community support. Affected personnel came from bases across the country, including the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry

“Those we lost, those who were injured, were training to defend Canada, to serve Canada. And now Canada serves them. … They will not carry it alone. Because in Canada, we take care of one another.” 

(Flags at half-mast; support pledged for families and the injured) @MarkJCarney

2111652303854076191.text:
🇨🇦 People have been killed and injured in an incident at Canadian Forces Base (CFB) Wainwright in Alberta that set off a major fire, Canada's Defence Minister David McGuinty said on Saturday night. He gave no casualty figures and no cause.

Prime Minister Mark Carney called it a "serious incident creating a major fire". Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said the "significant and tragic" fire is affecting many military personnel. Member of Parliament Dane Lloyd said he was hearing of "significant casualties" after an explosion and fire.

Strong winds pushed the fire across the base fence, the Municipal District of Wainwright said, and an emergency coordination centre has opened. Emergency Health Services is on scene providing care and transport.

McGuinty said the Canadian Armed Forces and the Department of National Defence will share more in the coming days. The base is about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton.

Sources: CBC; Global News; Associated Press; CTV News

2111689401051103636.text:
A serious incident at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, Alberta, on October 17 has resulted in fatalities and injuries, according to Defence Minister David McGuinty.

The Canadian Armed Forces reported that a fire was reported on the training range around 4 p.m. MT. Driven by high winds, the fire spread beyond the base boundary into the surrounding Municipal District of Wainwright. No evacuation orders were issued, but emergency services from multiple jurisdictions responded.

McGuinty confirmed that people were killed and injured but did not provide numbers or details on the cause. He described the situation as “very active and delicate” and said he could not recall a comparable incident in recent memory. The Canadian Armed Forces and RCMP are investigating. Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith have been in contact regarding the response.

Edmonton hospitals activated Code Orange mass-casualty protocols to prepare for patients being transported from the area.
Background context on the base includes a documented history of natural gas wells on the property (roughly 180 wells were reported in 2014) and the presence of live-fire ranges, pipelines, and munitions storage areas. Some local and online accounts have speculated that an artillery round struck a gas well, triggering a large explosion and secondary detonations, but these details have not been confirmed by official sources. NASA FIRMS satellite data has also been referenced in connection with thermal hotspots in the Peterson Pond–Jamieson Lake area on October 17.

Authorities continue to investigate the cause of the incident and the full extent of the casualties.

Praying for those involved this is only 4 hours from me.

Pilar Sanders told a court Deion Sanders was worth $250 million. Her prenup capped her at $1 million.

The agreement was signed on April 19, 1999. They married two days later.

The terms: $100,000 for each year of marriage, capped at $1 million. Her own lawyer from 1999 testified she also received a $100,000 "signing bonus" to sign it.

Deion filed for divorce in December 2011, after 12 years and three children.

The court record:
$24,000 a month in payments was what she asked for.
$10,500 a month in child support plus $275,000 for her lawyers was what a judge ordered in May 2012.
The child support was later cut to $2,500, then raised to $4,500.
On October 24, 2012, Judge Ray Wheless ruled she signed the prenup voluntarily and told her lawyers not to bring the claim again.
In March 2013, an arbitrator confirmed both of them signed it.
On March 12, 2013, a jury voted 11 to 1 to give Deion sole conservatorship of their two sons.

Her lawyers said parts of the prenup were forged, two pages were missing, and she signed under pressure. They wanted a handwriting expert to examine the original.

When she put his net worth at $250 million in court, Deion laughed out loud. By then a judge had ordered her to stay 500 yards away from the house she had lived in.

The case for Deion: she signed it, took the $100,000, and a judge and an arbitrator both upheld it. "This is greed. That's all it is," he said at the 2012 hearing. In 2013 he said, "It's not about the kids. It's about the money."

The case for Pilar: 12 years, three children, and a fixed $1 million against a fortune she estimated at $250 million, set two days before the wedding.

In the video below, in April 2012, she says: "I understand that I have very little chance at beating a Hall of Fame, two-sport man that everyone seems to love and adore."

My coworker's mother passed away last November.

He called the state health department, frantic, asking how a hospital stay could bankrupt an inherited home that had no mortgage balance.

The caseworker sighed and told him:

"Federal law requires state programs to claw back healthcare costs from deceased estates. The house cannot be sold or transferred until the balance is cleared in full."

He offered to pay a monthly settlement.

They said no. The full $114,000 is due in 60 days, or they foreclose on the property at a public auction.

A lifetime of working-class savings, wiped out overnight by a retroactive healthcare lien.

You don't own generational wealth.

You're just holding a property title until the state finds a legal mechanism to repossess it the moment you die.

2111493691496108272.text:
A game stops being fun the moment telling the truth becomes dangerous and refusing a dare could cost you everything.

Truth or Dare (2012) is a British supernatural horror thriller directed by Robert Heath. It follows a group of university students whose night of drinking and playing a familiar party game turns into a terrifying experience when their choices begin carrying consequences they never expected.

What makes the premise unsettling is how ordinary the game feels at first. Friends tease each other, secrets come out, and people push boundaries for a laugh. But once the atmosphere changes, every question feels like a trap, and every dare becomes a test of how far someone will go to protect themselves.

Compared with Would You Rather (2012), which turns a deadly game into a brutal examination of desperation and moral compromise, Truth or Dare leans more heavily into the fear of being exposed and losing control. Both films use games to strip away people’s comfortable masks, but Would You Rather makes its choices feel especially cruel because survival and morality collide so directly.

The strongest part of Truth or Dare is its simple, relatable setup: most people have played some version of this game. That familiarity makes the shift from harmless fun to genuine terror effective. However, the film doesn’t always develop its characters enough to make every revelation hit as hard as it could.

Rating: 6/10. Worth watching if you enjoy low-budget horror, psychological pressure, and stories where one bad decision leads to another.

Here’s the uncomfortable question: When a game forces you to choose between revealing your darkest secret and doing something you would normally refuse, which option would scare you more? And which movie handles deadly choices better: Truth or Dare or Would You Rather?

2111819651764166844.text:
Jordan Love was 14 when he lost his dad. The @packers QB remembers him and how he was one of his biggest supporters: “My dad actually wanted to name me Michael Jordan. That’s real. Michael Jordan Love. My mom vetoed it, thank God.

When I say my dad taught me everything, I really mean everything. We’d be out in the yard from the time I could walk — no, really from the time I could stand. Football, basketball, every sport imaginable. There’s a picture of me from when I was a baby and my dad is putting me up on a race horse. I’m like one, in my diaper, and I’m chilling up on some Secretariat-looking dude.

My dad’s motto was, ‘Try everything.’

He just had this relentless positivity about him. In his mind, me and my sisters could really do anything.

Him and my mom were both police officers. My dad was a sergeant for the Bakersfield Police Department and my mom was California Highway Patrol, but they couldn’t have been more different personalities. The smile never left my dad’s face. My mom, she was the yin to his yang. She was all business. She had an aura, you know? And that aura said, ‘Did you do your homework?’

Me and my friends would be out in the yard playing capture the flag or whatever, and she’d come home from work rocking those police aviators, and all my boys would be shook.

‘Don’t you boys have a pop quiz tomorrow?’

‘Yo, how’s she even know about that???’

One of those moms. You know the type.

My dad, he was my road dog. He used to pick me up after working a double shift and we’d pull up straight to the Little League field in his police cruiser. He’d be in the outfield helping coach with his full BPD uniform on, beeper in the belt buckle and everything. Everybody in town knew ‘Big O.’ Everybody loved him.

He was literally always just there.

Part 2, and my last post about my Shawn Ryan Show episode.

Last I heard, it had been edited. Then Shawn went on Diary of a CEO and described a woman whose interview he’d never release. That woman wasn’t me, unless he was lying.

But I never expected it to air, and here’s why:

I spent weeks prepping with Shawn’s team. I was booked to follow the money on TPUSA and the surveillance state, and naming names is what I do. I’m meticulous, and I never say anything I can’t prove. Then, right before we started filming, I was told I couldn’t name names. When I brought up who funds Flock Safety, the license plate cameras now in thousands of American towns, I was told not to say Andreessen Horowitz or Peter Thiel. You can’t follow the money without showing where the money flows. That’s when I realized this episode would never air, before we had even started.

So when I got home, I did what I do. I followed the money. And, turns out Shawn Ryan is invested in companies backed by the exact people I was told not to name, plus Israel.

(1) Anduril Industries: Ryan has been an investor since October 2025. Anduril started with surveillance towers and now builds drones and autonomous weapons. Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund led its June 2025 round, and Andreessen Horowitz co-led its $5 billion round in May 2026. Those are the two names I was told to leave out. In February 2026, Anduril’s founder, Palmer Luckey, made an undisclosed trip to Israel and met with Netanyahu and senior defense officials. By June, Anduril was setting up an Israel operation to sell to Israel’s Ministry of Defense. Shawn had Palmer on his show in February 2025 and invested eight months later.

(2) Shield AI: Ryan has been an investor since November 2025. It builds AI-piloted drones and fighter jets. Andreessen Horowitz led its first major round and has kept investing ever since. Shawn had its co-founder on the show the same season he invested.

(3) Sesh: Ryan has been an investor since August 2025. Its $40 million round was led by 8VC, the venture firm of Joe Lonsdale, who co-founded Palantir with Peter Thiel. Lonsdale was a guest on Shawn’s show on May 7, 2026, less than three months before I taped. Palantir signed a strategic partnership with Israel’s Ministry of Defense in 2024.

And Flock Safety, the company I came to talk about, is backed by Andreessen Horowitz, which led two of its rounds, and by Founders Fund, Peter Thiel’s fund.

So I was booked to expose who funds the surveillance state. I was told not to name Andreessen Horowitz or Peter Thiel. And the host has money in companies backed by Andreessen Horowitz, by Thiel’s fund, and by Thiel’s Palantir co-founder, including one that is building its business in Israel.

Then there’s the rest of it. Sarah Adams, his former network host, was messaging his team to keep me off (see Part 1 if you missed it). An IDF settlement contractor tagged the two of them together. Pro-Israel groups passed around her clip from his show as proof that Israel didn’t drive the war. And after his Diary of a CEO interview, accounts from the same network that spent the summer smearing me told everyone his “CIA woman” was me, citing “sources.” It wasn’t me. I never discussed a polygraph with Shawn Ryan, and it was never why I went on. So either he was talking about someone else, or somebody turned his story into a weapon against me.

Honestly, I don’t want the episode to air, and I told them so right after we taped, because it was a watered-down version of my work. How it all happened was a tough lesson learned for me in this industry. Now you know what was going on behind the scenes. If this episode doesn’t air, I can assure you it’s not because I’m a fraud. It’s because I won’t water down who funds the surveillance state, and I won’t sell out to protect anyone’s investments.

So there you have it.

A few years ago, Ashu had a high-paying corporate job in London, earning millions. Saurav was writing about the country’s legal system and living a great life. Both had successful careers, financial security and every reason to continue living the lives they had built for themselves.

But they chose to give it all up in the hope of making this country a better place. They had absolutely no reason to leave behind their comfortable lives, take to the streets, face uncertainty and eventually end up in jail. Yet they did.

What I admire most about these two is that despite coming from privileged backgrounds, they chose to fight for those who aren’t as fortunate. They could have easily looked the other way, enjoyed their lives and never bothered about the struggles of people they had never even met. Nobody asked them to make these sacrifices. Nobody expected them to. But they did, because they genuinely care about people beyond themselves.

And to me, that is the greatest quality a human being can have. To stand up for people you don’t know, to fight battles that aren’t your own, and to risk everything you have so that someone else might have a better life.

That’s the kind of people Ashu and Saurav are.

This is the publicly known Jalen Hurts timeline:

• The team says he was cleated in the calf vs. the Rams in Week 4 but didn't ask for treatment until a few days later, practicing in full in between.

• After the #Eagles flew to London, an ultrasound found a superficial blood clot in his calf. Doctors still cleared him to play.

• However, the night before the game, he spent time in the hospital and was told not to sleep because it was a risk. He played the full game without much sleep.

• He then took the roughly 7-8 hour flight from London back to Philly and started practicing in full that week. Speaking to the media, Hurts called it a "very unique experience" but didn't want to get into details.

• A follow-up ultrasound then showed the clot had moved, and he was ruled out for Week 6.

• Further testing has now diagnosed him with deep vein thrombosis and blood clots in both lungs. He's on blood thinners and expected to miss the rest of the season.

This is the absolute LAST post I ever expected to be making on the Monday of my bodybuilding show week.

After months of weighing every gram of food, tracking every calorie, hitting my workouts, doing my cardio, practicing my posing, and preparing myself mentally, physically, and spiritually to step on stage this Saturday, I spent this past weekend binge eating in a way I’ve never experienced before.

And when I say binge eating, I don’t mean I went out and enjoyed a cheat meal or ate a little more than I was supposed to.

I mean I completely lost control.

I kept eating long after my stomach was telling me to stop. I was physically uncomfortable, I wasn’t even enjoying the food anymore, and yet I continued eating.

And the scariest part wasn’t even the amount of food I consumed.

It was what was going through my head while I was doing it.

At a certain point, it felt like I was intentionally sabotaging myself. Like there was a part of me that wanted to ruin everything I had worked so hard for.

And I’ve spent the last couple of days asking myself WHY.

Was I afraid I wasn’t going to look good enough on stage? Was I afraid of disappointing myself? Was I putting so much pressure on myself that I subconsciously wanted a way out?

I don’t have all the answers.

But those are some uncomfortable questions I’ve had to start asking myself.

After the first binge, I told my coach Chris Elkins everything. Every single thing I ate. We talked about it, and the plan was to move forward, reassess, and take things day by day.

The next day, I got right back to my routine. Tracked my food, followed my plan, and genuinely thought I had moved past what happened.

Then nighttime came.

What started as one extra bite of food turned into another binge. And this one was even worse than the first.

I can’t even explain how disappointed I felt afterward.

Not because I had eaten food that wasn’t on my plan. But because I had reached a point where I felt like I couldn’t stop myself from doing something I knew was hurting me.

I woke up physically miserable. My face was extremely swollen, my body felt awful, and I was looking at myself in the mirror trying to understand how I had gotten here.

And now here I am.

Five days away from the competition I’ve spent months preparing for, roughly 10 pounds heavier than I was going into the weekend, and genuinely uncertain whether I’m going to step on stage this Saturday.

Chris believes competing is still an option. Part of me wants to finish what I started. Another part of me wonders whether postponing until November would be the better decision.

Because I know how much work I put into this prep. And I also know that the choices I made this weekend have consequences.

I’m not going to sit here and blame anybody else. I’m not going to pretend it didn’t happen. And I’m definitely not going to ask anyone to feel sorry for me.

But I also don’t want to spend the rest of my life beating myself up over two days.

I made those choices. I have to own them. And now I have to figure out how to move forward.

One thing this weekend has forced me to recognize is just how much pressure I’ve been putting on myself. Not only with bodybuilding, but with life in general.

Constantly working. Constantly thinking about what’s next. Constantly being on my phone. Constantly feeling like I need to be doing MORE.

And somewhere along the way, I stopped giving myself enough room to just live.

So regardless of whether I compete Saturday or in November, some things are going to change.

I’m prioritizing my sleep. I’m taking real breaks from social media. I’m giving myself time to recover. And I’m going to take a serious look at my relationship with food and the pressure I’ve been putting on myself.

I’m not going to pretend I’ve figured everything out in 48 hours. I haven’t.

And I don’t want to turn this into some inspirational story about how I fell down and immediately got back up stronger than ever.

I’m still figuring it out.

2112256359022362891.text:
Thanks to Trump accounts tweak, Musk can give every child SpaceX shares even if parents object

Elon Musk announced he will give every child in the United States stock in his company SpaceX, a maneuver that is possible thanks to the implementation of the Trump Accounts program.

Musk, the founder of SpaceX, Tesla, and other ventures, made the announcement Monday morning. He holds billions of shares of SpaceX.

“Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America,” Musk said on his social media platform, X. “This will be the first of many.”

The announcement follows the Treasury rolling out new rules that will allow charities to donate individual stocks to children’s Trump Accounts. Notably, parents cannot refuse the stock contributions, and those stocks can’t be sold for five years.

The Trump administration is taking public comment on the ability for parents to opt out of Trump Accounts.

Trump Accounts are tax-deferred investment savings accounts designed for children, to which parents, family members, and others can contribute money. The funds can be tapped into after the beneficiary turns 18.

In his message on X, Musk didn’t give any indication about how shares of SpaceX will be distributed. He owned some 4.8 billion shares of SpaceX when the company went public this year.

As of Monday morning, a single share of SpaceX was valued at just over $150.

For babies born between Jan. 1 of this year and Dec. 31, 2028, the government will deposit $1,000 into each Trump Account. That $1,000 cannot be touched until the beneficiary turns 18.

People can contribute up to $5,000 a year up until the year before the child turns 18.

Also, several companies have said they will match the $1,000 contribution from the government for eligible children. And employers of children or a child’s parent are allowed to contribute up to $2,500 per year to the accounts.

Source: https://t.co/ClBNFLv0SH

2112227716183277635.text:
Elon Musk posted on X early Monday morning: “Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many.” He didn’t say how the shares would be handed out or who would qualify, and CNBC reported it has reached out to SpaceX and Musk’s family office for details.

The numbers are big. There were about 72 million Americans under 18 as of July 2025, according to Census data cited by CNBC (CBS News and CNN put it near 73 million). At SpaceX’s Friday closing price of $146.03, CNBC figures that comes to about $10.5 billion in stock. CBS News reported SpaceX shares rose 2.7% to $149.49 Monday morning, a day before the company reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday.

The pledge came right after Anthropic, the AI company, announced Sunday it will put 5% of its shares into a new public benefit fund. Musk replied on X that he recommends giving shares directly to the public, and said that’s what he will be doing. CBS News noted the shares could go through the new Trump Accounts, the tax deferred savings accounts for children born from 2025 through 2028 that get a $1,000 government deposit, since Treasury rules let donors put stock into them. In July, SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell and her husband pledged one SpaceX share to each of roughly 2 million kids already signed up, putting lower income families and Texas kids first, CNN reported.

What’s next: no details yet on timing, eligibility or how families would claim a share. CNBC and CNN also pointed out Musk has made big giving promises before that didn’t happen, like his 2021 offer of $6 billion to the UN World Food Programme.

Now that’s how you share the wealth. No middleman, just a real piece of an American company for every kid. Put it in the Trump Accounts and let it grow. I hope the details come through soon. Thoughts?

Sources: Elon Musk on X, CNBC, CBS News, CNN

Feeling great is my #1 priority.

Mental clarity is my #1 priority

This is awesome 😂

This sounds insane until you’ve been on enough date nights where you spend $250 to discuss the kids’ schedules in a different building.

The backstory is pretty great!

A married couple in San Diego wanted to get dressed up and go to a wedding. Problem was, they’d reached the age where nobody they knew was getting married anymore.

So they built a website where you can buy tickets to strangers’ weddings.

And the economics actually make sense.

The couple getting married has already committed to a venue minimum. Someone cancels. Now there’s an empty chair and a dinner they’re paying for either way.

Meanwhile, another couple would happily pay to eat, dance, have some cake and watch a best man make a series of increasingly questionable decisions with a microphone.

The hosts approve the guests. Guests verify their IDs. Everybody agrees to the arrangement.

Which is arguably more vetting than your cousin’s new boyfriend received.

Apparently one bride said the paying strangers brought so much energy to the dance floor that she wished she’d invited more.

Of course they did. Those people specifically bought tickets to be there. Half your actual guests are attending under a treaty negotiated between their mothers.

I love businesses like this. Find something people already paid for but can’t fully use. Find someone else who wants it. Make the introduction.

This guy just wanted to take his wife dancing and accidentally identified a liquidity problem in the wedding market.

Cue Vince Vaughn!
