The ugly truth about France and some of the other European countries currently in turmoil - and which none of the politicians want to admit because it'd be political suicide - is that you can't solve the problem by going after immigrants (as the right asserts) or the rich (as the left asserts), but you could solve it by going after the old.

One extraordinary statistic for you: people over 60 in France, a quarter of the population, own 60% of France's wealth, non-financial and financial (https://t.co/IdJ5X7OO12).

And here is another crazy statistic: 
that same quarter of the population, those above 60, receive nearly two-thirds of all social spending by the French government (https://t.co/deNRNevIwq) - which is famously among the highest in the world (France's government spending is an insane 57.3% of GDP).

Last statistic: they make up about 40% of voters because they're a third of registered voters (https://t.co/zTa4RnVOmT), and they turn out far more than anyone else (https://t.co/34V2xzs9jH).

Put our 3 statistics together and there's almost a bit of an apartheid situation here: the old own most of the country's wealth, collect most of the social spending and have the political power to keep it that way.

Which makes them a de-facto rentier class, living off assets and transfers paid for by younger generations.

And, of course, at the risk of stating a truism, the future is built by the young. Yet France keeps effectively taking money away from them to give it to those whose working lives are already behind them - and need the money far less since they already own the country's wealth.

What about inheritance, I hear you ask? That's the funniest/saddest aspect: given that life expectancy has kept rising, the French now inherit a home at 54 on average. The most common case is someone in their 80s leaving it to heirs in their 50s, in effect the very old transferring wealth to the about-to-be old (https://t.co/d2RPAqLJGR). 

You can add this to our earlier apartheid statement: on top of all the rest, even when the old finally let go of their wealth, it stays within their own "camp".

That's my personal situation, incidentally: I'm 42, my father is 71 and he is starting to look at ways to pass things on to me and my siblings, when our professional lives are already well settled, so it'll arrive when it changes things the least, which is pretty much the French system in a nutshell.

Now, I get that there'd be some unfairness in going after them: they paid into the system their entire working lives, playing by the rules of a social contract that told them if they paid up they'd collect at the end. Changing the rules now means breaking that promise, which is admittedly unfair.

But there's no magic wealth tree in any society: you can only take it where it is. That's the way most major societal transformations end up happening. They're often triggered by a catastrophic event (the so-called "four horsemen": mass-mobilisation war, revolution, state collapse, plague) BUT what really drives change is a transfer: wealth gets pried from the privileged class who've been sitting on it and handed to those who'll build what comes next.

So, in theory and in an ideal world, you can do without the catastrophic event and directly proceed with the transfer...

The fact that in France, and elsewhere in Europe, it's the youth protesting is probably no coincidence - even though they don't frame it as a generational fight. And even though, cruel irony, the left politicians many of them march behind promise to bring the retirement age back to 60 (https://t.co/WrJOhpWqYR), which would make the situation even worse.

Let's say they understand intuitively that the system is stacked against them, even if they haven't yet figured out how. And politicians are obviously doing what politicians do, meaning pandering to the people who actually vote, while pointing the young towards easier - and politically convenient - scapegoats.

To be clear I'm not saying it's the only problem in France, VERY far from it. I'm also not saying that all old people in France live a lavish lifestyle at the expense of younger generations: there are also plenty of very poor retirees who, if anything, would deserve more.

What I am saying is that it's probably the biggest elephant in the room: everyone can see it, nobody dares mention it - no politician, from any side, wants to run on cutting grandma's pension - and it makes every other problem harder to fix.

A eleitora deixa o colégio, e a gravação termina.

A eleitora vestia uma camisa amarela da Seleção e um boné do Maga, movimento de apoiadores do presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump. As someone with a portfolio of energized land assets here is what I am seeing:

1. Neoclouds are disorganized and poorly capitalized. Some are definitely better than others however. 

2. Hyperscalers are intractable, bureaucratic organizations that take 3 months to do an NDA and want 18mo escrow periods. We built our portfolio by competing against these terms because of our speed and simplicity. The more future assets orgs like ours win, the bigger the problem for the hyperscalers downstream (see 3). 

3. There are delays in the existing pipeline that will catch people off guard in 2027. Hyperacalers will (obviously) react by focusing on their own internal compute needs over any third party. If the third party is a model company, they will tell them to go through their model router where they will also take a non-trivial vig. Them telling Ant they have no compute for them (rumored in Ant’s S-1) if true is a huge tell that this is already happening. 

All of this is to say that it does look like there will be a lot of partially stranded compute and compute sitting in inventory in 2027 than is currently forecasted. This is bought and paid for but effectively underearning (below total cost of capital) or collecting dust. We see this as true for everyone - model companies, hyperscalers, neoclouds except ONE (you can guess which one). 

This dislocation will benefit two kinds of orgs: the non-bureaucratic big scalers who can build industrial scale quickly and the nimble, well capitalized players feeding them. 

2027 will be a turbulent year because it will clear out a bunch of wrong/bad bets. It will also be a consolidation year for a few.

I'm a plus-sized woman, and a man I'd been talking to for three days took me on what I thought was the best first date of my life. Then he sent me a photo from that date with a caption I still can't believe.

His name was Tyler. We matched on a Tuesday, and by Wednesday we were texting all day. He sent good morning messages, shared pictures of his lunch, and remembered little things I'd told him. Talking to him felt effortless.

On Friday, I asked if he wanted to FaceTime. He answered immediately.

“There she is,” he said, smiling. “Wow. You look exactly like your pictures.”

He complimented my eyes, my hair, and my skin. He called me beautiful and asked me to spend Saturday with him.

“Come to my hotel in the morning,” he said. “We can spend the whole day together.”

I wasn't comfortable going to a hotel room with someone I'd known for three days, so I suggested breakfast at my usual café instead.

He agreed without complaining.

The next morning, I arrived to find him waiting at our table. He stood up when he saw me and pulled out my chair.

For the next two hours, he was everything I'd hoped he'd be. He made me laugh, asked questions, and actually listened to my answers.

When I ordered pancakes, eggs, and bacon, he smiled.

“Good. I hate when women order salads on dates just to impress someone.”

I laughed. For once, I wasn't worrying about how I looked while eating.

There was just one thing I noticed. His phone was propped against the sugar dispenser, its camera pointed directly at me.

When I glanced at it, he turned it over.

“Sorry, work's blowing up,” he said.

I believed him….

¿BUKELE Y SU WATERLOO?

Con el anuncio del envío hacia Haiti, desde El Salvador, de un contingente de 3000 militares, cuya misión es encontrar a los 4 miembros de las fuerzas armadas de ese país, secuestrados el pasado domingo, cuando penetraron en territorio dominado por las pandillas y fueron atacados por una pandilla de irregulares armados, se avizoran en las próximas horas fuertes enfrentamientos armados.

A estas horas, y sabiendo cómo se resuelven las cosas en Haití, las probabilidades de que estos militares continúen vivos son mínimas, así que si no hay posibilidad de negociar nada, y por lo tanto lo que se plantea es un enfrentamiento armado entre tropas de El Salvador y las pandillas que son dueñas del territorio donde fueron atacados y secuestrados los militares centroamericanos.

Según lo publicado en la prensa internacional, los responsables son dos organizaciones criminales que dominan el área de “Croix des Bouquets”, una de ellas dirigida por Claude Celestin, quien es cabeza de la pandilla Chen Mechan (perros rabiosos), y Wilson Joseph (“Lammo San Jou) líder de la banda 400 Mawozo.

En el día de ayer, este último desafió públicamente  al presidente Nayib Bukele en un vídeo publicado en las redes sociales, donde advirtió que no se irá de Haití, y mostró miles de municiones y pertrechos con arma de diversos calibres, que según el están esperando a los salvadoreños.

Tenemos entonces la bandeja servida para un enfrentamiento armado a solo 45 kms de la frontera de la República Dominicana y Haití, de un ejército de pandilleros armados sin nada que perder, frente a tropas regulares de El Salvador, que pelearán una guerra urbana en las calles de un país que no es el suyo y es absolutamente desconocido.

Ya en el pasado reciente, los Estados Unidos en 1994 mando 20,000 soldados e intentó organizar a Haití para que se volviera a la senda de lo que ellos llaman democracia, y luego en el 2004 invadieron de nuevo junto a Canada, lo que terminó en la creación de una fuerza multinacional, la Minustah, que terminó en el más absoluto fracaso, es decir, estamos metidos en un tema que no tiene solución.

Si hay alguien que tiene experiencia en combatir pandillas lo es Nayib Bukele, el presidente de el Salvador, su historia de combate a las “Maras” está a la vista de todos, solo que Haití no es el terreno amigo donde peleó esa guerra, un país de habla y cultura hispana donde jugaba de local, el país caribeño es un transplante de África en América, con una historia de violencia típica de las sociedades primitivas.

Cuando Napoleón envió a sus tropas a sofocar la revolución haitiana en 1802, pensó que miles de solados podrían devolver la colonia a sus dueños, pero solo un año después, Dessalines y la fiebre amarilla los obligó a rendirse, ¿será Haití el Waterloo de Bukele?.

El futuro dirá.

Before they died, late Access Bank co-founder Herbert Wigwe and the wife, Chizoba, bought a yacht, which was a shiny toy for them. 

The yacht was named after their first daughter, Otutochi, who ironically is the person today managing the vast wealth that the parents left behind on behalf of the surviving siblings who are younger than her. 

The yacht was a 2016 Custom Line 108 luxury yacht measuring approximately 33 meters (108 feet) in length, and the cost of acquiring it was $6.5 million. 

The yacht primarily served Herbert, his wife, and his close friends anytime they wanted to escape from the reality of the daily life hustle by relaxing and sailing  on the sea. 

The yacht was also deployed for charter for big boys and girls who can afford to rent it. 

The yacht was purchased in 2016, and to escape the wahala that comes with tax, an offshore company, Grosvenor Marine Ventures Ltd., a company registered in the British Virgin Islands (BVI), was incorporated. 

The offshore company was owned by the late Herbert and the wife, and the offshore company's only asset was that luxury yacht. 

Herbert is no more, the same with the wife.

Tochi, the 26-year-old finance graduate who is the heiress to the wealth that the parents left behind, is struggling to maintain the luxury yacht.

The annual cost to own and maintain a luxury yacht typically ranges from 10% to 20% of the vessel's initial purchase price

Main Expense Categories

Crew Salaries: Often the single largest expense, scaling from a small self-operated team to full-time staff costing anywhere from $300,000 to over $1.4 million for mid-size vessels and $1.5 million to $4 million+ for superyachts. 

Routine Maintenance & Upkeep: Accounts for 2% to 10% of the yacht's value annually (covering engine servicing every 100–200 hours, bottom paint, hull cleaning, and HVAC repairs). 

Periodic dry-docking and major refits are required every few years. 

Fuel: Varies heavily by engine power and usage. Larger motor yachts can burn hundreds of gallons of diesel per hour while cruising, easily running into $400,000 to $1 million+ a year. 

Berthing & Dockage: Marina slips range from $30,000 to over $500,000 annually depending on the vessel's length and the prestige of the port (e.g., Mediterranean vs. local marinas). 

Insurance: Comprehensive marine, hull, and third-party liability (P&I) policies cost roughly 0.5% to 2% of the yacht's total value per year (spanning from $30,000 to $500,000+). 

So since the parents died, Tochi has been struggling to keep up with the cost because the asset in question is a depreciating asset. 

At the beginning of this year. She made the difficult decision to sell the yacht because the estate the parents left behind can no longer afford to maintain it. 

It is taking too many resources from her and the estate she is managing on behalf of her surviving siblings. 

But there was a problem. 

The offshore company that her parents floated was no longer active, as it had been dissolved because, since the parents died, the offshore company has stopped filing at the jurisdiction it was registered in. 

So Tochi had to approach  the High Court of Justice of the British Virgin Islands (BVI) to secure control of a company holding a luxury yacht belonging to her late parents.

She also paid the necessary debt the offshore company was owing before the status of the company was restored for the transaction of the sale of the luxury yacht to be completed. 

The luxury yacht was sold in Florida for the sum of $6.5 million, and the money remitted to the estate that Tochi is controlling on behalf of her siblings 

$6.5 million is 8.7 billion naira. 

Herbert  was a very wealthy man in his lifetime. 

I wonder how he managed to stay under the radar that the public did not know he was this wealthy until he was no more.

I’m sure Tochi would have been astounded by the staggering wealth that the late dad left behind....👇

I’m a content creator and pole dancer, and dance is one of the things that makes me feel most like myself. But I currently practise outdoors on our balcony because our ceiling isn’t suitable for mounting my pole indoors. The sun, rain and weather conditions constantly interrupt my training.

Having a place of my own where I could safely install my pole, practise consistently, create content and develop my craft would mean the world to me.

Sir, I’m not asking for a luxury lifestyle. I’m asking for a chance to stand on my own feet, feel safe, and reconnect with the woman I know I can become.

If you could help me secure a place of my own and get this new chapter started, it would mean more to me than I can explain. I know you must receive countless requests, but I hope you can hear the sincerity in mine.

Thank you for even taking the time to read this, sir. ❤️🙏🏽
